titles.Neighbouring organs: Bladder, urethra, ureters, rectum and anus

clinical: Pelvic shape in childbirth
The size and shape of the bony pelvic inlet and outlet set the passage a baby must pass through during labour.
Slipped disc at L5/S1
A herniated lumbosacral (L5/S1) disc, with L4/5 the other common site, can press on a spinal nerve root and cause back pain radiating down the leg (sciatica).
Pelvic organ prolapse
Weakened levator ani and supporting tissue, often after vaginal childbirth, can let the bladder, uterus or rectum sag down into the vagina. This is called prolapse.
Stress incontinence
Pelvic floor weakness is a common cause of stress urinary incontinence, where urine leaks on coughing, sneezing or lifting.
Fibroids
Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are benign smooth muscle tumours of the myometrium, common in women of reproductive age. They can cause heavy periods and pelvic pressure.
Postpartum haemorrhage
After delivery the myometrium must contract to compress the vessels of the placental site. Failure to contract (uterine atony) is the commonest cause of severe bleeding after childbirth.
Cervical screening
Most cervical cancers arise in the transformation zone, where squamous and columnar epithelium meet. This is the area sampled at cervical screening.
HPV infection
Almost all cervical cancers are caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV).
Vaginal atrophy after menopause
Falling oestrogen after the menopause thins the squamous lining of the vagina, causing dryness, soreness and painful intercourse.
Ectopic pregnancy
Most ectopic pregnancies implant in the uterine tube, usually in the ampulla, and can rupture causing severe internal bleeding.
Salpingitis
Infection of the tube can scar and block it, causing infertility and raising the risk of ectopic pregnancy.
Polycystic ovary syndrome
A common hormonal disorder that causes irregular ovulation and raised androgen levels. The ovaries often show many small peripheral follicles on ultrasound.
Ovarian torsion
The ovary can twist on its blood-vessel pedicle, cutting off its blood supply and causing sudden severe pelvic pain that needs urgent surgery.
Uterine prolapse
The cardinal and uterosacral ligaments help hold the cervix and uterus in place. Stretching of these supports, together with pelvic floor weakness, contributes to uterine prolapse.
Round ligament pain
Sharp pain in the groin during the second trimester is often round ligament pain, caused by stretching as the uterus enlarges.
Endometriosis

Endometriosis is growth of endometrial-type tissue outside the uterus. It commonly implants on the pelvic peritoneum, including the rectouterine pouch, and on the ovaries, causing pelvic pain and sometimes infertility.
Fluid in the rectouterine pouch
Blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, or pus, can collect in the rectouterine pouch and can be felt on vaginal examination of the posterior fornix.
Bleeding after childbirth
Severe postpartum bleeding can be controlled by embolising the uterine arteries, which is less invasive than tying the internal iliac arteries.
Ureter injury in hysterectomy
The ureter runs beneath the uterine artery close to the cervix, so it is at risk of injury during hysterectomy.
Urinary tract infection
The short female urethra lies close to the vagina and anus, making urinary tract infection, especially cystitis (bladder infection), much more common in women than men.
Bladder injury at caesarean section
The bladder sits in front of the lower uterine segment and can be injured during caesarean section, especially where there are adhesions.
Bartholin's cyst
Blocked Bartholin's (greater vestibular) glands can form a painful cyst or abscess beside the vaginal opening.
Perineal tears
Tears of the vestibule and perineal body are common in vaginal childbirth, and both tears and episiotomies are repaired in layers.
Breast cancer
Most breast cancers arise from the ducts or lobules. A tumour that pulls on the suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments can dimple the overlying skin.
Mastitis
A blocked lactiferous duct in a breastfeeding woman can become infected, causing a red, painful breast (mastitis).
Ovarian cancer
Ovarian epithelial tumours, the most common ovarian cancers, were long thought to arise from this surface layer. They are often diagnosed late because early symptoms are vague.
Hilus cell tumour
Rare hilus cell tumours of the ovary can produce androgens, causing virilisation such as facial hair and a deeper voice.
Scarring from salpingitis
Infection of the tube can scar and fuse the mucosal folds, blocking the lumen and trapping the embryo, which can cause ectopic pregnancy.
Asherman's syndrome
Scarring of the endometrium, often after curettage or uterine surgery, causes thin or absent periods and can lead to infertility.
Endometrial cancer
Endometrial cancer typically presents with abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding, so any such bleeding needs investigation.
Fertile window
Conception is only possible in the few days before ovulation and about a day after it. The egg survives about 24 hours, while sperm can survive several days in the female tract.
IVF
In IVF the egg is fertilised in a laboratory dish and the embryo is transferred to the uterus, often at the blastocyst stage.

parts.description: The fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) is the lowest mobile vertebra of the spine, sitting on the sacrum at the lumbosacral angle, where the lower back meets the pelvis. Its body is large and wedge-shaped, taller in front than behind, and its spinous process is short and rectangular, which helps identify it. It carries much of the weight of the upper body and is joined to the sacrum by the L5/S1 intervertebral disc.

The lumbosacral intervertebral disc (L5/S1) lies between the body of the fifth lumbar vertebra and the upper surface of the sacrum. Like other discs, it has a tough outer ring of fibrocartilage (the anulus fibrosus) around a soft, gel-like centre (the nucleus pulposus), which cushions the spine and absorbs shock. It is wedge-shaped, thicker in front, because of the lumbosacral angle, and together with L4/5 it is the commonest level for disc prolapse.

The fundus of the uterus is the rounded upper dome of the body, lying above the points where the uterine tubes enter. In pregnancy its height above the pubic symphysis (symphysis-fundal height) is measured to follow foetal growth. Its wall is thick myometrium, a layer of interlacing smooth muscle that contracts strongly in labour and after delivery.

The functional layer (stratum functionalis) is the superficial two thirds of the endometrium, the lining of the uterus. It contains coiled uterine glands in a cellular stroma, with spiral arteries that reach towards the surface. Under oestrogen it thickens in the first half of the cycle; after ovulation, progesterone makes the glands secrete and the stroma prepare for implantation. If pregnancy does not occur, falling progesterone makes the spiral arteries constrict and this layer is shed as menstruation.

The cervical canal is the narrow, spindle-shaped (fusiform) passage through the cervix, running from the internal os above to the external os below. It is lined by simple columnar, mucus-secreting epithelium, and in pregnancy it is filled by a thick mucus plug that forms a barrier against infection travelling up from the vagina. This plug is expelled as the 'show' at the start of labour, when the cervix begins to dilate.

The internal os is the narrow upper opening of the cervical canal, where the canal meets the cavity of the uterus at the level of the isthmus. It marks the boundary between the cervix and the body of the uterus. In a section, the endocervical mucosa, with its branching folds (the arbor vitae), gives way to the endometrium, which has simple tubular glands in a cellular stroma.

The vaginal canal is the potential space inside the vagina, the lumen between its anterior and posterior walls. Normally these walls lie against each other, so in cross-section the collapsed canal forms a transverse H-shaped slit. The walls are pushed apart during intercourse and childbirth, and the upper canal opens out around the cervix, which projects into it to form the fornices.

The urinary bladder is a hollow muscular reservoir that stores urine until it is passed. It lies behind the pubic symphysis and in front of the uterus and cervix, its base resting against the anterior vaginal wall. Its wall is made of detrusor smooth muscle, which contracts to empty it, and is lined by urothelium, a transitional epithelium that is largely impermeable to urine. In pregnancy the enlarging uterus presses on it, causing frequency of micturition.

Urine is the fluid that collects in the bladder lumen after the kidneys filter the blood and the ureters carry it down. It is mostly water, with urea, salts and other waste products. The bladder stores it until the detrusor contracts and the sphincters relax to pass it through the urethra, and as the bladder fills the urge to void grows.

The coccygeus (ischiococcygeus) is a small, triangular muscle forming the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm. It runs from the ischial spine to the side of the lower sacrum and coccyx, lying on the sacrospinous ligament. It is supplied by branches of the S4 and S5 nerves and, together with levator ani, supports the pelvic organs and helps pull the coccyx forwards.

The ampulla of the uterine tube is the widest and longest part of the tube, lying on the lateral side between the isthmus and the infundibulum. Its wall is thin and its mucosa forms a labyrinth of branched folds, which helps identify it in a section. Fertilisation normally takes place here within about 24 hours of ovulation. It is also the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy, and a ruptured tubal pregnancy bleeds into the peritoneal cavity and can cause shock.

The infundibulum of the uterine tube is the funnel-shaped lateral end of the tube, opening into the peritoneal cavity close to the ovary, and its rim is fringed with fimbriae. The fimbriae sweep the ovulated oocyte into the tube, and one long fimbria, the ovarian fimbria, is attached to the ovary. Infection that ascends from the cervix, such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea, can reach the tube, causing salpingitis and tubal infertility, and can spread out through the open end into the peritoneal cavity.

The abdominal ostium is the wide opening at the free end of the infundibulum, the funnel-shaped lateral end of the uterine tube, where the tube's lumen connects with the peritoneal cavity. An ovulated oocyte enters the tube through this opening, swept in by the fimbriae around its rim. Because the opening links the tube to the peritoneal cavity, infection can pass from the tube into the abdomen through it.

The ovary is the female gonad, an almond-shaped organ lying in the ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall, behind the broad ligament. It produces oocytes and the steroid hormones oestrogen and progesterone. It is held in place by the mesovarium, the ovarian ligament and the suspensory ligament, and its surface becomes scarred with age from repeated ovulation. Torsion, a twist of the ovary on its vascular pedicle, causes sudden, severe lower abdominal pain.

The internal iliac artery is the principal arterial supply of the pelvis, arising from the common iliac artery at the level of the sacroiliac joint and descending into the pelvis. It divides into anterior and posterior divisions; the anterior division gives off the uterine, vaginal and vesical arteries. It supplies the pelvic organs, the perineum and much of the gluteal region, and its branches may be embolised to control severe post-partum haemorrhage.

The uterine artery, a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, runs medially in the base of the broad ligament. It crosses over the ureter about 2 cm lateral to the cervix, a relation that matters at hysterectomy. Near the uterus it divides into an ascending branch, which anastomoses with the ovarian artery, and a descending cervicovaginal branch. Arcuate arteries supply the myometrium, and their radial branches feed the straight and spiral arteries of the endometrium.

The ovarian artery is a branch of the abdominal aorta, arising just below the renal arteries at about the level of L2. It runs down on the psoas muscle, crosses the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim and enters the suspensory ligament to reach the ovary through the mesovarium. Its tubal branch anastomoses with the uterine artery, linking the ovarian and uterine blood supplies.

The vesicouterine pouch is a shallow peritoneal recess lying over the isthmus, between the bladder in front and the anterior surface of the lower uterus. At caesarean section the peritoneum here is opened to reach the lower uterine segment, with the bladder pushed down out of the way.

The labia majora are two large, prominent folds of skin containing fat and smooth muscle, running from the mons to the perineum and enclosing the pudendal cleft. Their outer skin is hair-bearing and contains sebaceous, sweat and apocrine glands, and the round ligament of the uterus ends in them. They are the homologue of the scrotum, and their lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, the route by which vulval cancer spreads.

The mons pubis is the rounded pad of subcutaneous fat lying over the pubic symphysis, at the front of the vulva. The skin over it bears pubic hair after puberty, and the fat cushions the pubic symphysis against pressure. The two labia majora run back from it, so it marks the upper limit of the vulva on examination.

The pudendal cleft (rima pudendi) is the slit between the two labia majora, running from the anterior commissure, at the front below the mons pubis, back to the posterior commissure near the perineum. When the labia are parted it opens into the vestibule, and when they are closed it appears as a vertical line that marks the entrance to the genital tract.

The prepuce of the clitoris, or clitoral hood, is the fold of skin formed where the lateral limbs of the labia minora join above the clitoral glans. It shields the glans from friction and contact, and it is the female counterpart of the penile foreskin. The glans lies beneath it and is exposed only when the hood is drawn back.

The perineal body, also called the central tendon of the perineum, is a fibromuscular node between the vaginal orifice and the anus, where the bulbospongiosus, the superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles and the external anal sphincter meet. It can be felt on vaginal examination just behind the introitus. It is the central part of the clinical (obstetric) perineum, the soft tissue between the vaginal opening and the anus, and it is stretched or torn in childbirth.

The greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands are pea-sized mucous glands lying behind and to the side of the vaginal orifice, beneath the bulb of the vestibule. Their ducts open into the vestibule in the groove between the hymen and the labia minora, and their secretion lubricates the vestibule during sexual arousal. A blocked duct forms a Bartholin cyst, which can become infected and form an abscess. They are the homologue of the bulbourethral (Cowper) glands.

The tunica albuginea of the ovary is a thin layer of dense connective tissue lying just beneath the germinal (surface) epithelium and covering the ovarian cortex. Its closely packed collagen fibres make it pale, which gives the ovary its whitish colour. In a section it is the dense band that separates the surface epithelium from the cortex and its follicles.

The theca externa is the outer layer of the theca, the sheath of connective tissue that wraps around a growing follicle. It is made of concentric collagen fibres and fibroblasts, with some smooth-muscle-like cells, and it merges gradually with the surrounding ovarian stroma. Their possible contraction may help push the oocyte out of the follicle at ovulation. In a section it forms the outer, fibrous rim of the follicle, outside the more cellular and vascular theca interna.

The theca interna is the inner, vascular layer of the theca, lying outside the basement membrane of the granulosa cells. Its cells carry LH receptors and make androgens such as androstenedione, which the granulosa cells convert into oestradiol under FSH stimulation. In a section it is a cellular, highly vascular ring of stroma that lies just inside the more fibrous theca externa. Excess androgen production by theca cells is a key feature of polycystic ovary syndrome.

The antrum is the fluid-filled cavity that forms inside a secondary follicle as small spaces in the granulosa layer join together. It contains follicular fluid (liquor folliculi), rich in oestradiol, proteins and hyaluronan, and it enlarges under FSH as the follicle grows. The cumulus oophorus projects into it, carrying the oocyte at one side. In a section, look for a clear, pale space ringed by granulosa cells.

The cumulus oophorus is the mound of granulosa cells that projects into the antrum and holds the oocyte, attached to the wall of the follicle. Its cells are joined by gap junctions and embedded in a hyaluronan (hyaluronic acid) matrix, which swells under the LH surge and loosens the mass. At ovulation the cumulus disperses, and the oocyte leaves surrounded only by its innermost layer, the corona radiata. In a section, look for a bulge of granulosa cells projecting into the fluid-filled antrum.

The central clot, or corpus haemorrhagicum, is a blood clot that fills the cavity of the follicle just after ovulation, in the centre of the young corpus luteum. The clot is gradually organised by fibrin and invading fibroblasts, and is then resorbed and replaced by connective tissue. In a section, look for a red-stained blood clot in the middle of a young corpus luteum, surrounded by the yellowish lutein cells.

The corpus albicans is the white, scar-like remnant left when a corpus luteum degenerates. It consists of dense, hyaline (glassy) collagen with few cells, and it lies in the ovarian stroma where the luteal tissue used to be. It may persist for months to years, slowly shrinking as it is resorbed. In a section, look for a pink-staining, sparsely cellular scar of dense collagen where a yellow corpus luteum once was.

An atretic follicle is one that degenerates by apoptosis (programmed cell death) instead of ovulating, and most follicles undergo atresia at some stage. The oocyte and the granulosa cells break down first, while the zona pellucida, which thickens and becomes wavy, is the last part to disappear. In a section, look for a shrunken follicle with a degenerating oocyte and a collapsing wall, and note the thickened, wavy zona pellucida as a helpful clue.

The theca of a secondary follicle is the sheath of ovarian stromal cells that condenses around the granulosa layers as the follicle grows. It differentiates into two parts: the inner theca interna, which is cellular, vascular and makes androgens, and the outer theca externa, which is more fibrous. A thin basement membrane separates the whole theca from the granulosa. In a section, the theca appears as a ring of stroma around the granulosa, cellular on the inside and fibrous on the outside.

Primordial follicles are the smallest follicles, each a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I of meiosis since fetal life, surrounded by a single layer of flat follicular cells. They form the resting pool in the outer cortex of the ovary, and a few are recruited to grow each day. In a section, look for a small round oocyte with a large pale nucleus, ringed by a thin layer of flattened cells, just beneath the ovarian surface.

Oocytes are the female germ cells; the primary oocytes stay arrested in prophase I of meiosis from before birth until shortly before ovulation. At the LH surge, the oocyte completes meiosis I, throws off the first polar body and is ovulated as a secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II. This secondary oocyte completes meiosis only if a sperm enters it. In a section, look for a large round cell with a big, pale nucleus, central in a primordial or primary follicle and within the cumulus of an antral follicle.

The corona radiata is the innermost layer of the cumulus, made of granulosa cells arranged radially around the zona pellucida. It is the layer that accompanies the ovulated oocyte, and sperm must pass through it before they can reach the zona. Sperm disperse these cells with hyaluronidase released from their acrosome. In a section, look for a single ring of radially oriented cells round the zona of an oocyte.

The mesovarium is the posterior part of the broad ligament, a double layer of peritoneum that attaches the anterior border of the ovary to the ligament. The ovarian blood vessels and nerves run between its two layers on their way to the hilum of the ovary. This arrangement keeps the ovary suspended from the broad ligament while its free posterior border projects into the peritoneal cavity.

The ovarian arteries in the medulla are branches of the ovarian artery that enter the ovary at the hilum and coil through the medulla as helicine (coiled) arteries. Their branches run outward to supply the cortex and the thecae of growing follicles. The ovarian artery also anastomoses with the uterine artery, giving the ovary a second route of blood supply.

The ovarian veins drain the medulla and follow the arteries out through the hilum of the ovary. Here they form the pampiniform plexus, a network of thin-walled veins within the suspensory ligament of the ovary. The right ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava and the left into the left renal vein.

The areola is the ring of thin, pigmented skin that surrounds the nipple, and it darkens during pregnancy. Beneath the epidermis it contains smooth muscle fibres, which help the nipple stand erect, and numerous sebaceous glands. In a section, look for pigmented epidermis over a dermis rich in smooth muscle and sebaceous glands.

The areolar glands, also called the glands of Montgomery, are small sebaceous glands that rise as tubercles on the areola. Although they are sebaceous glands, they also contain some rudimentary mammary tissue. Their oily secretion lubricates and protects the nipple during breastfeeding. They can be seen as small raised bumps on the areola.

A lobe of the mammary gland is one of 15 to 20 radially arranged compound glands, each with branched tube-and-sac secretory units and drained by its own lactiferous (milk) duct towards the nipple. Neighbouring lobes are separated by fibrous septa and fat, and each lobe is made up of many lobules. Seen in section, the lobes look like clusters of glandular tissue fanning out from the nipple through a fatty stroma.

The lactiferous sinuses are the dilated parts of the lactiferous ducts just deep to the areola, traditionally described as small milk reservoirs before the nipple. Ultrasound studies of lactating women suggest they are branching ducts rather than distinct sacs, so the reservoir role is debated. In a section, look for expanded duct segments directly beneath the nipple.

The ribs are twelve pairs of curved bones that form the bony cage of the thorax and protect the lungs and heart. The breast lies over the 2nd to 6th ribs and the intercostal spaces between them. Each rib has a head, neck and shaft, with a costal groove along its lower border that carries the intercostal vessels and nerve. Carcinoma of the breast can invade the chest wall, including these ribs.

The intercostal muscles fill the spaces between the ribs, with the external intercostal the most superficial of the three layers, lying deep to pectoralis major at the level of the breast. They move the ribs during breathing and are supplied by the intercostal nerves. The anterior perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery pierce these muscles to supply the medial breast.

Axillary lymph nodes are the group of nodes lying in the armpit (axilla), mostly around the axillary vein. They filter lymph from the upper limb, the breast and the skin of the upper trunk, and are grouped as levels I to III by their position relative to the pectoralis minor muscle. Because most breast lymph drains here, sentinel node biopsy of this group is used to stage breast cancer.

The serosa of the uterine tube is its outer covering, formed by the peritoneum (the lining of the abdominal cavity) that wraps around the tube within the mesosalpinx, the part of the broad ligament that carries it. Histologically it is a single layer of flat mesothelial cells resting on a thin layer of loose connective tissue, which carries the blood vessels and nerves to the tube. Its smooth surface lets the tube slide against neighbouring organs with little friction.

The muscular layer of the uterine tube is its smooth muscle wall, made of an inner circular coat and a thinner outer longitudinal coat. It is thin in the ampulla, the wide section of the tube, and thick in the isthmus, the narrow segment next to the uterus. Together with the cilia of the lining, its peristalsis moves the early embryo along the tube towards the uterus, a journey that takes about 3 to 4 days.

keys: Mucosa of uterine tube (lamina propria folds)
parts.description: The mucosa of the uterine tube is the inner lining, thrown into longitudinal folds (plicae) that run along the length of the tube. In the ampulla these folds are tall and branched, forming a labyrinth with only narrow clefts of lumen between them, and each fold has a core of loose connective tissue (lamina propria) beneath its epithelium. The folds greatly increase the surface area of the ciliated and secretory epithelium, which moves and nourishes the gametes and embryo.

The blood vessels of the uterine tube wall are small branches of the ovarian and uterine arteries, which join up (anastomose) in the mesosalpinx and then run into the lamina propria (the loose connective tissue under the lining) and muscle coat. In a section they look like small arteries and veins scattered among the smooth muscle bundles and the loose connective tissue.

The inner layer of the myometrium is the innermost smooth muscle of the uterus, lying directly beneath the endometrium. Its bundles interlace in several directions, and radial arteries pass through it on their way to the endometrium. In a section, look for dense, interlacing smooth muscle just below the endometrial glands, with thick-walled vessels among it. Like the rest of the myometrium, its contractions expel the fetus in labour and compress the vessels after delivery to limit bleeding.

The stratum functionalis is the superficial, thick part of the endometrium, the layer that is shed at each menstruation. It lies above the stratum basalis, is lined by the uterine surface epithelium, and thickens under the influence of oestrogen and then progesterone. In the secretory phase its stroma becomes oedematous, its glands turn saw-toothed and secretory, and its spiral arteries coil; in a section these coiled arteries distinguish it from the straight vessels of the deep basal layer.

Straight (basal) arteries are the short branches of the radial arteries that run straight down into the stratum basalis, the deep layer of the endometrium. Unlike the spiral arteries, they do not respond to ovarian hormones or constrict at menstruation, so the basal layer survives and regenerates the functional layer. In a section, their straight course, without the coils seen in the spiral arteries, tells them apart.

The chorionic cavity (extraembryonic coelom) is the fluid-filled space lying inside the chorion, the outer membrane of the conceptus. The amnion and yolk sac hang within it from the connecting stalk, and the cavity is gradually obliterated as the expanding amnion fills it. In a section it appears as the space between the chorion and the amnion, lined by loose extraembryonic mesoderm.

The amniotic sac (amnion) is the thin, transparent membrane that encloses the amniotic cavity and, later, the whole embryo and fetus. It forms in the second week from amnioblasts, flattened cells that arise from the epiblast, and it expands to fill the chorionic cavity as the embryo grows. In a section it appears as a single layer of flat cells lining the amniotic cavity, with no blood vessels in it.

The amniotic cavity is the fluid-filled space enclosed by the amnion, lying directly above the epiblast (the upper layer of the embryonic disc). It appears in the second week as small spaces within the epiblast join up, and it enlarges until it surrounds the developing embryo. Its fluid cushions the fetus, allows the free movement needed for normal joint and muscle development, and lets the lungs grow and mature.

The hypoblast (primitive endoderm) is the lower, cuboidal layer of the bilaminar embryonic disc, facing the yolk sac. It arises from the inner cell mass in the second week and lines the yolk sac as extraembryonic endoderm. During gastrulation in the third week it is displaced by definitive endoderm migrating from the epiblast.

The connecting stalk is the band of extraembryonic mesoderm that tethers the embryo to the chorion. It carries the allantois, a small outgrowth of the hindgut, and the umbilical blood vessels, and it develops into the umbilical cord that later links the fetus to the placenta. In a section it is recognised as a mesodermal strand running from the embryo to the chorion, containing blood vessels.

The corona radiata is the layer of cumulus cells that remains around the ovulated oocyte, attached to its zona pellucida (the glycoprotein coat). Its cells are radially arranged and linked to the oocyte by processes that cross the zona. Sperm must pass through this layer first, using the enzyme hyaluronidase carried in the sperm head and the beating of their tails.

Sperm cells are the male gametes: small cells with a condensed haploid nucleus in the head, a midpiece packed with mitochondria, and a tail that propels them. Once capacitated in the female tract, a sperm passes the corona cells, binds to ZP3 in the zona pellucida and undergoes the acrosome reaction, releasing enzymes that let it penetrate the zona. Only one sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane, which triggers the cortical reaction (a block to polyspermy) and completes meiosis II.

The zona pellucida is the thick, transparent glycoprotein coat that surrounds the oocyte and then the early embryo, lying outside the cell membrane. Before fertilisation it binds sperm through its ZP3 protein, and afterwards it keeps the blastomeres together and prevents the embryo attaching to the wall of the uterine tube. In a section it appears as a clear band that stains pink with eosin, and the blastocyst hatches from it at about day 5-6 before implanting.

The zygote is the single diploid cell formed when the sperm and oocyte nuclei fuse, normally in the ampulla of the uterine tube about a day after ovulation. It has extruded its second polar body, and its cytoplasm is almost entirely maternal, since the sperm contributes little more than its nucleus and centriole. Its first cleavage division follows about 30 hours later, so in a section it is a single cell beside a small polar body within the zona pellucida.

The female (egg) pronucleus is the haploid nucleus of the oocyte, formed when the oocyte completes meiosis II after the sperm has entered it. It carries the maternal set of 23 chromosomes and stays separate from the male pronucleus until the two are brought together on the first mitotic spindle. In a fertilised egg it is seen as one of two pale, round nuclei.

The 2-cell stage is the first cleavage stage, reached about 30 hours after fertilisation, when the zygote divides into two blastomeres (cells) still enclosed in the zona pellucida. Cleavage divides the cytoplasm without increasing the overall size of the embryo, so each blastomere is smaller than the zygote was. The embryo keeps dividing into 4-cell and 8-cell stages as it travels down the uterine tube.

The morula is the compact, solid ball of 12 to 32 blastomeres that forms about 3 to 4 days after fertilisation; its name comes from its resemblance to a mulberry. It is still enclosed in the zona pellucida as it passes along the uterine tube and enters the uterine cavity. In a section it is a cluster of cells with no fluid-filled cavity, which distinguishes it from the later blastocyst.

The trophoblast of the blastocyst is the outer, single layer of flattened cells that surrounds the blastocyst, formed around day 5 of development. Unlike the inner cell mass, which forms the embryo itself, these outer cells go on to form the fetal part of the placenta, and they attach to and invade the endometrium at implantation. In a section it is recognised as the thin outer rim of flat cells encircling the blastocyst cavity.

The blastocele (blastocyst cavity) is the fluid-filled space inside the blastocyst, which forms about day 4 of development. Its walls are formed by the trophoblast (the outer cell layer), which pumps fluid into the cavity, except at one pole, where the inner cell mass projects into it. In a section it appears as a clear space lying off-centre, which enlarges as the blastocyst grows until the blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida and implants at about day 6-7.
